Bulungula Update

By: Catherine Rice | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In September last year, we investigated a crime wave sweeping the picturesque Wild Coast in the Eastern Cape. In the months since our story aired, the crime has continued unabated.

Unique Selling Point:
We investigated a terrifying crime wave sweeping the picturesque and remote Wild Coast in the Eastern Cape. Since our story aired in September, crime has continued unabated. Despite promises of increased police visibility in the area, there has been no assistance for communities living in fear.

Summary:
Tony and Jean Robertson were attacked last year and were featured in our first story. In this update, we interview them again. They were attacked for the second time in just eight months in February. Tony was shot in the leg and foot, his wife pistol whipped. Both are severely traumatised. They had increased their security, but their alarms did not frighten off the intruders who escaped with their cellphones and iPads. They had also hired a night watchman who ran away when two gunmen pointed a firearm at him.



Further information:
Tourism in the area has taken a massive knock, with bookings at the 100 percent community owned Bulungula Lodge down. This is impacting the entire community. It's not just the tourism sector on it its knees, the development sector too is under threat.

Script:


VO 1 Six months ago, we visited the Nqileni Village on the Wild Coast. It had been just weeks since an attack on Dave Martin and his wife Rejane Woodroffe.

VO 2 CCTV footage captured part of their terrifying ordeal. Tied up and kidnapped in the vehicle owned by their non profit organisation, the Bulungula Incubator, they were later released. But, not without suffering significant trauma.

VO 3 They weren’t the only ones affected by a crime wave sweeping the region. A few months before, another couple we met had been attacked in their home and now - just eight months later - it’s happened again.

VO 4 Coffee Bay, Mdumbi, Hole in the Wall - these are just some of the popular tourist destinations affected.

UPSOUND Tony Robertson: What worries me is who’s going to be next? 21:47 Where does it stop?

VO 5 Now, as the situation appears to have gone from bad to worse, we’re back to ask what the future holds for these communities under siege, and to investigate whether the police have delivered on their promise to increase visibility?

FADE TO BLACK

VO 6 Andiswa Tshayiso is the manager of the one hundred percent community owned Bulungula Lodge.

VO 7 Over the years, thousands of tourists have visited here. But, as violent criminals started to infiltrate the area just over a year ago, bookings began to plummet.

UPSOUND Andiswa Tshayiso / Bulungula Lodge Manager: Since last year, here at Bulungula has changed, because of the high crime happening on the Wild Coast.

MASA: All over the Wild Coast?

UPSOUND Andiswa Tshayiso: All over the Wild Coast, it’s happening.

VO 8 The tourism sector, the lifeblood of this fragile economy, has been brought to it’s knees.

UPSOUND Andiswa Tshayiso / Bulungula Lodge Manager: Here, its very very bad. Everyone is very, very sad in the community because like the bookings are cancelled, there is no money will come. And we in trouble. Like, the Bulungula Lodge depend to the tourists who are travelling, if no one is travelling, we in trouble I can say. Even the community itself. And there’s no money to pay the salaries for the staff.

LINK Being back this time around, it’s quite different, there’s a sense of defeat and fear that lingers. And it’s quite tragic.

VO 9 Investigations have stalled, cases have gone cold, and the community feels more isolated than ever.

VO 10 One of the victim’s in last years attacks was Lindiwe Tukane. She too was kidnapped from her home and later released in a forest. Like Dave and Rejane, she’s left the area - for now.

UPSOUND Tony Robertson: First thing I remember is just seeing this silhouette of this guy coming into the bedroom. I thought no, not again man.

VO 11 Tony and Jean Robertson live in neighbouring village, Mpame. In April last year, they were savagely beaten in their home for a small amount of cash and electronics. Tony’s car was also stolen and later recovered – completely stripped.

VO 12 And then last month, despite security upgrades, they were attacked again.

UPSOUND Tony Robertson: It was a really nice day. Jean had made a nice dinner. First thing I remember is Jean running into the bedroom. I heard the siren going off and she just said “people are trying to break in”.

VO 13 CCTV footage shows two men prowling around buildings on the Robertson’s property.

VO 14 The night watchman they’d hired, runs away after one of the attackers points a gun at him. One of the attackers flees, but the other stays behind.

UPSOUND Tony Robertson: And as I walked in, the sliding door was laying on its side, and Jean was on the floor. And the guy said to me get on the floor.

VO 15 It was about to get much worse.

UPSOUND Tony Robertson: I heard these two shots, I turned around. I could smell the gunpowder. Jean says he was dragging her by her hair. And I looked down and I saw the blood. That’s when he kicked me continually in the face. He’d ask a question, he’d kick me.

MASA So he actually shot you?

UPSOUND Tony Robertson: Ja he did, ja, ja twice. One shot was through my foot, just below the ankle and came out the bottom. The other one was through the left calf.

VO 16 Since the attack, Tony and Jean have left Mpame, unsure of when - or if - they will return.

UPSOUND Tony Robertson: You know, as my brother said, last time you got hit on your head. Sorry.

Masa: It’s OK Tony.

UPSOUND Tony Robertson: This time you’ve been shot, next time you’re dead.

VO 17 So what are the police doing about it? Seemingly, not very much.

UPSOUND Tony Robertson: Something has to be done. I feel that the local police are incapable of doing anything.

VO 18 Communities have been lobbying for police intervention. In September last year, they protested outside the Elliotdale police station demanding more police visibility.

VO 19 And not long after that, they received a mobile police station, in the form of a large truck.

LINK This mobile police station has been here since about October last year. Problem is it’s randomly manned. Sometimes there’s police officers here, most of the time not. Like now.

VO 20 Unmanned and immobile for months - it now serves as a shelter for goats.

VO 21 And while a new police station is under construction nearby, progress is slow.

UPSOUND Andiswa Tshayiso: There’s no one that’s working in there. The police must be around all the time to patrol, all the time to check us. No one is arrested, they just like come and do what they want to do. No one is arrested.

VO 22 Until that happens, or at the very least cases are properly investigated, the safety of residents here hangs in the balance.

UPSOUND Tess Peacock: A lot of us who have lived here don’t feel safe to live here anymore.

VO 23 Tess Peacock is the director of the Equality Collective, a social justice organisation that cultivates active citizenry to improve service delivery. One of their projects improved water supply for local communities, significantly.

UPSOUND Tess Peacock / Director: Equality Collective: That really galvanised around 33 volunteers across forty villages to really take responsibility for the water services and started messaging every day whether there was water or not. In the end we worked very constructively with the government to try and improve the services. And today the scheme is refurbished. It’s gone from 40 percent reliability index in kind of 2022 to ninety percent now.

VO 24 She says it’s not just tourism that’s under threat from the spike in crime, it’s the development sector too.

UPSOUND Tess Peacock / Equality Collective Director: We’ve got over ninety percent unemployment rate. This is one of the poorest parts of South Africa. And when you have such a fragile economy that hinges on things like tourism, any development needs a safe space right, but particularly tourism. It does deeply affect us, and particularly our ability to attract talented, skilled staff members who want to come and work in a region like this.

MASA Have you had people who’ve moved?

UPSOUND Tess Peacock: Most of our critically skilled staff who are not from this community originally, we’re all kind of living outside of the village at the moment.

VO 25 Working remotely has become the safer option.

UPSOUND Tess Peacock: It’s clearly organised crime. And what that requires is an intelligent targeted police response. We’re just not seeing that. If we call the police they’ll come ten hours later. There’s no security services, there no private security services. We’re exceptionally vulnerable out here.

VO 26 The community policing forum does what it can - nightly patrols across the length and breadth of the village.

NATSOUND Walkie Talkie

UPSOUND Tess Peacock: The fact that the community has galvanised in such a beautiful way reminds us why we want to be here. But, we really do need the state and the police to do their part.

LINK We’ve been trying to get an interview with the acting provincial police commissioner for weeks now. They did agree to an online interview. Then started giving us the run around. So now we wait.

VO 27 Our scheduled zoom interview was cancelled, then rescheduled and we were told to be on standby. Finally, we were informed there was no time in the acting provincial police commissioner’s schedule.

VO 28 His name is Zithulele Dladla - a major-general recently appointed to tackle crime in the province.

VO 29 But, if his track record is anything to go by, that appointment doesn’t bode well. Back in 2014, when he was the station commander of Khayelitsha’s Site B police station, a commission of inquiry, set up to investigate allegations of police failures in the township, found serious inefficiencies. These included poor detective work and a lack of regular patrols.

VO 30 Despite promising to email a statement in response to our questions, Eastern Cape police failed to do so.

VO 31 For those directly impacted by crime in this region, the future remains uncertain until there is proper police action.

UPSOUND Andiswa Tshayiso: We the people we are because of Bulungula Lodge. If Bulungula die, we will die, there’s no future. Even, we don’t know when they will come, even someone opens the door we always very , very scared about that.

UPSOUND Tony Robertson: We feel like refugees in limbo. I mean, the Wild Coast was meant to be an idyllic place. Shoh, not anymore.
